RestoreDART sample size and filtering checks

BEM

September 2026

Notes

  • This document holds the per-objective detail: how much data backs each objective x cover response, what the three sample-size filters removed, and what that objective’s own results look like. It is written for deciding what the data can support, not for reporting conclusions - the collaborator-facing results are in 2_make_DART_results.Rmd, which carries the cross-objective direction checks and every table compiled across objectives. The bulky per-ecoregion reference graphs are in 2_raw_result_graphs.Rmd.

Each section covers one objective x cover response, in five parts:

  1. Sample sizes and scope - pixel counts per treatment x ecoregion cell and, post-filter, per treatment and per ecoregion; what each of the three filters removed; how much of this objective’s data is shared with other objectives.
  2. Pixel and polygon counts, post-filtering - the three count histograms.
  3. Significant DART effects, by covariate - the overall significance rate, then the same rate by fine objective, treatment and ecoregion.
  4. Significant DART effects, through time - significance by year since treatment, effect magnitude and peak years, and how per-polygon peak years distribute across treatments and ecoregions.
  5. Overall results and interpretation - that objective’s filtering statistics in one row, then the hand-written interpretation. The prose is the only part of a section that is not generated.

A final section, Overall results and interpretation, all objectives, closes the document: the filtering statistics for all five objectives in one table, and the five interpretations together. It is emitted from the same per-objective sources as the sections above rather than restating them, so editing a bullet in its own section updates both places.

Results after all three filters

The pixel cutoff for each (treatment × ecoregion) combination was 300.

Three filters have now been applied to this objective x cover response, in this order, and the percentage below is the combined cost of all three:

  1. Sparse (treatment x ecoregion) cells - the 20 combinations listed above, below 300 pixels each.
  2. Depopulated treatment or ecoregion levels - on, at the same 300-pixel threshold: 0 treatment and 0 ecoregion level(s) removed. This catches a level thinned across many surviving cells, which the cell filter cannot see.
  3. Late-year truncation - year 27 was the first below 10 significant pixels, so it and the 1 year(s) after it were dropped; the series now ends at year 26.

Total data lost across all three: 2.53%. Treatment levels absent from the post-filter data: soil disturbance, prescribed burn;seeding;soil disturbance, prescribed burn;seeding;soil disturbance;vegetation removal. Ecoregion levels absent: Eastern Mojave Low Ranges and Arid Footslopes, Malad and Cache Valleys, Crystalline Mid-Elevation Forests, Mid-Elevation Uinta Mountains. (These are levels gone for any reason - a level that only ever appeared in sparse cells disappears without the depopulation filter being involved.)

Significant DART effects, through time

The same effects along the time axis and against the covariates that interact with it: how often a significant effect occurred in each year since treatment, how large those effects were and when they peaked, and how the per-polygon peak years distribute across treatments and ecoregions. Read the two halves as separate questions - a year can carry a high significance rate with small effects, or the reverse.

How does time since treatment affect significance?

This section attempts to answer two questions:

  1. How often does a significant effect show up in a given year? The stacked-direction figure immediately below.

  2. How large are those effects? The mean-effect table and figure further down. A year can have a handful of significant pixels that each moved a long way, or many pixels that each moved a little, and those are different results.

No weighting is used anywhere in this section. The mean effect per year is a plain arithmetic mean of effect over the significant pixels in that year, split by direction of effect, so the reported peak is the year whose significant pixels actually moved furthest rather than a significance-weighted compromise across the whole time series. Some weighting methods were checked and did not improve the results - see weight_testing_summary.Rmd for that analysis.

Everything in this section is drawn on the truncated series: for this objective the record is cut at year 26, because year 27 was the first with fewer than 10 significant pixels. This is what stops a peak year being reported from the part of the record where almost nothing was significant; it also means the x axis here can end earlier than another objective’s, so the two are not read off the same range.

Figure. X axis: years since treatment, one bar per year, labelled every 5 years. Y axis: the percentage of that year’s pixels with a significant DART effect - the full height of a bar is the year’s overall % significant, and it is a percentage of all pixels observed in that year, not of the significant ones. Fill: the direction of the significant effect, splitting each bar into a blue significant negative component and a red significant positive component; the intended direction for this objective (negative) is the segment drawn against the axis, with the unintended direction stacked above it. Fill colours mean the same thing in every direction figure in this report. There are no facets or other groupings.

Two different sample sizes are labelled on each bar, and they are not meant to sum to each other:

  • The rotated label sitting above each bar is that year’s group total - every pixel observed in that year, significant or not. It says how much data is behind the bar, and it is the denominator of the percentage on the Y axis.
  • The white label inside each stacked segment is the number of pixels that were significant and in that segment’s direction. These two are the sample sizes behind the two segment heights themselves.

So the two segment labels add up to the number of significant pixels in that year, which is generally far smaller than the group total above the bar, because most pixels in a year are not significant. Reading down a tall bar with a small group total is therefore a different situation from a short bar with a large one, which is exactly why both numbers are drawn. Segments too short to hold their label legibly are left unlabelled to avoid white text spilling onto the panel background.

  • Treatment was most effective (highest % significant pixels) at year 1 (40.0% significant).
  • Treatment was least effective (lowest % significant pixels) at year 25 (5.7% significant).

Table. One row per direction of effect: the year in which the mean effect over significant pixels was largest in magnitude, that mean, its SE, the number of significant pixels behind it, the last year observed for that direction, and whether the peak is censored (lands on that last year).

Figure. X axis: years since treatment. Y axis: the mean DART effect (Δ RAP cover) among significant pixels only in that year, computed separately for each direction - so the two series sit either side of the zero line by construction and are never averaged into a single number. Colour: direction of the effect (red = significant positive, blue = significant negative), using the same colours as the stacked figure above. The shaded band around each line is that year × direction mean ± 1 SE: it is sampling uncertainty in the mean effect, not the spread of individual pixel effects, so it narrows mainly where a year has many significant pixels. A year × direction cell backed by a single significant pixel has no SE and is drawn as a bare point, keeping the line through it unbroken. Dashed vertical lines mark each direction’s peak year from the table above, labelled with the mean effect at the peak, its SE, and the number of significant pixels behind it. Non-significant pixels are excluded outright rather than entered as zeros, and no weighting is applied anywhere. There are no facets or other groupings.

  • Significant negative effects were largest at year 18 (mean effect -43.2565, SE 1.7902, n = 132 significant pixels).
  • Significant positive effects were largest at year 25 (mean effect 28.7774, SE 3.5268, n = 10 significant pixels).

Note that the year with the largest mean effect need not be the year with the most significant pixels: the two questions can peak at different times, and a peak that lands on the last observed year is flagged as censored above for the same reason as in the by-polygon table further down.

Tables. Each polygon is reduced to the single year in which its own % significant pixels was highest (“peak significance year”); those per-polygon peak years are then summarized across polygons, by treatment in the first table and by ecoregion in the second. Columns: number of polygons behind the row, mean / SD / min / max of the peak year, and the percentage of polygons whose peak fell on the last year they were observed. A polygon’s peak year is flagged as “censored” in those cases, because we can’t rule out that significance was still rising beyond the end of the available time series. Note that “last year observed” now means the last year retained after the late-year truncation described above, so where a series was truncated the censoring flag is partly an artefact of the threshold rather than of the record itself - it marks the end of the analysable series, not necessarily the end of the data. What that censoring implies is taken up under Interpretation at the end of the report.

Overall results and interpretation

Summary statistics

What the three sample-size filters cost this objective x cover response, in one row - the same quantities reported in prose under Results after all three filters above, gathered here so that this subsection stands on its own. The identical row appears in the cross-objective filtering log in 2_make_DART_results.Rmd, where it can be read against the other objectives.

Objective Cover Min Pixels per Tx x Eco # Tx x Eco Excluded # Tx Depopulated # Eco Depopulated Min Pixels per Year Year Truncated At # Years Dropped % Pixels Lost # Tx Absent # Eco Absent
decrease_afg AFG 300 20 0 0 10 27 2 2.53 3 4

Table. One row for this objective x cover response. % Pixels Lost is the combined cost of all three filters, not the cell filter alone. # Tx Absent / # Eco Absent count levels missing from the post-filter data for any reason, which is a different quantity from the two depopulated columns: a level that only ever appeared in sparse cells disappears without the depopulation filter being involved.

Post-filter, this objective x cover response retains 84175 pixels across 6 treatment level(s) and 14 ecoregion level(s), the smallest surviving totals being 977 pixels for a treatment and 666 for an ecoregion, against a per-cell threshold of 300.

Interpretation
  • This was the only objective that achieved mostly the opposite of what it intended in that the direction of effect was usually positive, while the attempted effect was negative. I would hypothesize that the very strong unintended-effect result has to do with disturbance effects or the interact effects of compound objectives.
  • Significance patterns over fine objectives are highly heterogenous, but too complex to interpret casually.
  • Significance patterns over treatments are also highly heterogenous, but similarily complex.
  • Significance patterns over ecoregion probably require some environmental context, or an expert eye. For example I don’t have enough personal knowledge to guess why Uinta Basin Floor was so much higher than the other ecoregions.”
  • Treatment was generally not successful.
  • CLAUDE: The unintended direction dominates by a factor of 4.2 (22.7% of pixels unintended against 5.4% intended), and it dominates in every year bin: the ratio narrows from 5.1:1 in years 1-5 to 2.2:1 at 16+ but never reverses. So the result is not an early transient that later resolves - it is the standing pattern for this objective across the whole record.
  • CLAUDE: The compound-objective explanation offered above is consistent with the overlap structure: only 5.68% of these pixels carry no other objective, while 79.17% also carry increase_pfg. This section is therefore not an independent sample - it is largely the same ground the other objectives report, read against a different goal.
  • CLAUDE: The ecoregion spread is driven by small cells and should be read as a hypothesis-generating list, not a ranking. The top ecoregion (Uinta Basin Floor, 25.79% intended) holds 1,008 pixels, 1.2% of this objective’s 84,175, while the pixel-weighted rate for the objective as a whole is 5.4%. Any statement about the objective should quote the weighted rate.
  • CLAUDE: Within the treatment axis the ordering is interpretable even if the levels are heterogeneous: vegetation removal ranks first at 14.06% intended, with 1 of 6 treatments above 10%, and the largest treatment by area - seeding, 27,645 pixels - returns 1.87%. Where intended reductions in annual grass did occur they involved physically removing or disturbing vegetation rather than seeding alone.
  • CLAUDE: Do not read timing off the peak-magnitude table for this objective. The intended peak (-43.3 at year 18) rests on 132 significant pixels and the unintended peak (28.8 at year 25) on 10, both late in a record truncated at year 27. The per-polygon peak-significance years are early by contrast (treatment means of 2.8-6.2 years), so the frequency of a significant effect peaks early and decays while the large late means come from very few pixels.

Significant DART effects, through time

The same effects along the time axis and against the covariates that interact with it: how often a significant effect occurred in each year since treatment, how large those effects were and when they peaked, and how the per-polygon peak years distribute across treatments and ecoregions. Read the two halves as separate questions - a year can carry a high significance rate with small effects, or the reverse.

How does time since treatment affect significance?

This section attempts to answer two questions:

  1. How often does a significant effect show up in a given year? The stacked-direction figure immediately below.

  2. How large are those effects? The mean-effect table and figure further down. A year can have a handful of significant pixels that each moved a long way, or many pixels that each moved a little, and those are different results.

No weighting is used anywhere in this section. The mean effect per year is a plain arithmetic mean of effect over the significant pixels in that year, split by direction of effect, so the reported peak is the year whose significant pixels actually moved furthest rather than a significance-weighted compromise across the whole time series. Some weighting methods were checked and did not improve the results - see weight_testing_summary.Rmd for that analysis.

Everything in this section is drawn on the truncated series: for this objective the record is cut at year 32, because year 33 was the first with fewer than 10 significant pixels. This is what stops a peak year being reported from the part of the record where almost nothing was significant; it also means the x axis here can end earlier than another objective’s, so the two are not read off the same range.

Figure. X axis: years since treatment, one bar per year, labelled every 5 years. Y axis: the percentage of that year’s pixels with a significant DART effect - the full height of a bar is the year’s overall % significant, and it is a percentage of all pixels observed in that year, not of the significant ones. Fill: the direction of the significant effect, splitting each bar into a blue significant negative component and a red significant positive component; the intended direction for this objective (negative) is the segment drawn against the axis, with the unintended direction stacked above it. Fill colours mean the same thing in every direction figure in this report. There are no facets or other groupings.

Two different sample sizes are labelled on each bar, and they are not meant to sum to each other:

  • The rotated label sitting above each bar is that year’s group total - every pixel observed in that year, significant or not. It says how much data is behind the bar, and it is the denominator of the percentage on the Y axis.
  • The white label inside each stacked segment is the number of pixels that were significant and in that segment’s direction. These two are the sample sizes behind the two segment heights themselves.

So the two segment labels add up to the number of significant pixels in that year, which is generally far smaller than the group total above the bar, because most pixels in a year are not significant. Reading down a tall bar with a small group total is therefore a different situation from a short bar with a large one, which is exactly why both numbers are drawn. Segments too short to hold their label legibly are left unlabelled to avoid white text spilling onto the panel background.

  • Treatment was most effective (highest % significant pixels) at year 1 (29.4% significant).
  • Treatment was least effective (lowest % significant pixels) at year 20 (6.9% significant).

Colour: direction of the effect (red = significant positive, blue = significant negative), using the same colours as the stacked figure above. The shaded band around each line is that year × direction mean ± 1 SE: it is sampling uncertainty in the mean effect, not the spread of individual pixel effects, so it narrows mainly where a year has many significant pixels. Interpretation
  • Treatment looked successful, but at a smaller magnitude than the other objectives
  • needs more details
  • CLAUDE: The frequency evidence supports the reading above: the intended direction outnumbers the unintended one 2.2:1 (10.3% against 4.7%), the second-narrowest margin among the four objectives whose result went in the intended direction, and the intended peak mean effect is -21.4 in Δ RAP cover units at year 1 (n = 2455 significant pixels).
  • CLAUDE: The objective-level rate is effectively one treatment’s rate on one ecoregion. prescribed burn carries 124,020 of the 186,596 pixels (66%) at 8.65% intended, and Semiarid Benchlands and Canyonlands carries 132,266 (71%) at 8.79%; the higher rates in those tables - seeding at 24.15% and Sagebrush Basins and Slopes at 29.45% - each sit on a few percent of the pixels. The 10.3% headline should be attributed accordingly rather than read as a general result for shrub reduction.
  • CLAUDE: The response is immediate and then erodes rather than building: the intended peak falls at year 1, the earliest of any objective, and the intended rate declines monotonically from 17.32% in years 1-5 to 6.54% at 16+. Nothing here suggests a lagged shrub reduction.
  • CLAUDE: Ignore the unintended peak of 14.2 at year 27 - it is backed by n = 1 significant pixels and has no SE, so it is a single-pixel artefact of averaging over significant pixels only, not a late reversal. The late-year truncation at year 33 does not catch it, because that filter counts across both directions.
  • CLAUDE: This objective has the thinnest polygon base of the five - 61 polygons across 11 treatments, with up to 50% of a treatment’s polygons censored at their last observed year - so the per-polygon peak-year summaries are indicative only. 95.41% of its pixels carry another objective (85.21% also increase_pfg), which means the shrub reduction cannot be separated from the treatments those objectives describe.

Significant DART effects, through time

The same effects along the time axis and against the covariates that interact with it: how often a significant effect occurred in each year since treatment, how large those effects were and when they peaked, and how the per-polygon peak years distribute across treatments and ecoregions. Read the two halves as separate questions - a year can carry a high significance rate with small effects, or the reverse.

How does time since treatment affect significance?

This section attempts to answer two questions:

  1. How often does a significant effect show up in a given year? The stacked-direction figure immediately below.

  2. How large are those effects? The mean-effect table and figure further down. A year can have a handful of significant pixels that each moved a long way, or many pixels that each moved a little, and those are different results.

No weighting is used anywhere in this section. The mean effect per year is a plain arithmetic mean of effect over the significant pixels in that year, split by direction of effect, so the reported peak is the year whose significant pixels actually moved furthest rather than a significance-weighted compromise across the whole time series. Some weighting methods were checked and did not improve the results - see weight_testing_summary.Rmd for that analysis.

Everything in this section is drawn on the truncated series: for this objective no year fell below the 10-significant-pixel threshold, so the full record to year 33 is used. This is what stops a peak year being reported from the part of the record where almost nothing was significant; it also means the x axis here can end earlier than another objective’s, so the two are not read off the same range.

Figure. X axis: years since treatment, one bar per year, labelled every 5 years. Y axis: the percentage of that year’s pixels with a significant DART effect - the full height of a bar is the year’s overall % significant, and it is a percentage of all pixels observed in that year, not of the significant ones. Fill: the direction of the significant effect, splitting each bar into a blue significant negative component and a red significant positive component; the intended direction for this objective (negative) is the segment drawn against the axis, with the unintended direction stacked above it. Fill colours mean the same thing in every direction figure in this report. There are no facets or other groupings.

Two different sample sizes are labelled on each bar, and they are not meant to sum to each other:

  • The rotated label sitting above each bar is that year’s group total - every pixel observed in that year, significant or not. It says how much data is behind the bar, and it is the denominator of the percentage on the Y axis.
  • The white label inside each stacked segment is the number of pixels that were significant and in that segment’s direction. These two are the sample sizes behind the two segment heights themselves.

So the two segment labels add up to the number of significant pixels in that year, which is generally far smaller than the group total above the bar, because most pixels in a year are not significant. Reading down a tall bar with a small group total is therefore a different situation from a short bar with a large one, which is exactly why both numbers are drawn. Segments too short to hold their label legibly are left unlabelled to avoid white text spilling onto the panel background.

  • Treatment was most effective (highest % significant pixels) at year 2 (39.7% significant).
  • Treatment was least effective (lowest % significant pixels) at year 24 (15.0% significant).

Colour: direction of the effect (red = significant positive, blue = significant negative), using the same colours as the stacked figure above. The shaded band around each line is that year × direction mean ± 1 SE: it is sampling uncertainty in the mean effect, not the spread of individual pixel effects, so it narrows mainly where a year has many significant pixels. Dashed vertical lines mark each direction’s peak year from the table above, labelled with the mean effect at the peak, its SE, and the number of significant pixels behind it. Note that the year with the largest mean effect need not be the year with the most significant pixels: the two questions can peak at different times, and a peak that lands on the last observed year is flagged as censored above for the same reason as in the by-polygon table further down.

What that censoring implies is taken up under Interpretation at the end of the report.

Interpretation
  • To be written.
  • CLAUDE: This is the strongest and cleanest result in the report. The intended direction outnumbers the unintended one 5.6:1 (25.6% against 4.6%) on the largest pixel base of the five (556,499), and it is the only objective where a substantial share of pixels - 38.12% - carries no other objective, so it is the one result that is close to an independent sample.
  • CLAUDE: Read its covariate tables with the threshold in mind. This objective’s per-cell floor is 10 pixels against 300 for the other four, and no cell, level or year was dropped (0.00% of pixels lost), so its treatment and ecoregion tables retain cells the other sections would have removed - the smallest surviving ecoregion row is 16 pixels. The extreme rates at the top of the ecoregion table are those cells; the pixel-weighted rate is 25.6%.
  • CLAUDE: The treatment ordering is the clearest management signal in the document. Every combination of seeding with mechanical work sits at the top - seeding;vegetation removal leads at 51.44% intended - while prescribed burn alone returns 11.59% on 154,865 pixels (rank 11 of 13) and the largest treatment by area, vegetation removal (218,327 pixels), returns 22.89%. Mechanical removal paired with seeding is 2.2 times the intended rate of removal alone and 4.4 times the rate of burning.
  • CLAUDE: The decay through time is the one finding that generalises across all five objectives, though what the unintended rate does alongside it differs: here the intended rate falls from 34.73% in years 1-5 to 11.89% at 16+ while the unintended rate rises from 2.82% to 6.88%, so the intended-to-unintended ratio collapses from 12:1 to 1.7:1. Detectable tree-cover reduction is a property of the first decade after treatment.
  • CLAUDE: The peak means are late (-26.6 at year 29 intended, 14.2 at year 31 unintended) but rest on 100 and 27 significant pixels against 556,499 in total, and no year was truncated here, so the tail of the record is retained at very small per-year samples. Treat the peak years as poorly determined and lean on the year-bin table for timing instead.

Results after all three filters

The pixel cutoff for each (treatment × ecoregion) combination was 300.

Three filters have now been applied to this objective x cover response, in this order, and the percentage below is the combined cost of all three:

  1. Sparse (treatment x ecoregion) cells - the 27 combinations listed above, below 300 pixels each.
  2. Depopulated treatment or ecoregion levels - on, at the same 300-pixel threshold: 0 treatment and 0 ecoregion level(s) removed. This catches a level thinned across many surviving cells, which the cell filter cannot see.
  3. Late-year truncation - no year fell below 10 significant pixels, so the series was not truncated.

Significant DART effects, through time

The same effects along the time axis and against the covariates that interact with it: how often a significant effect occurred in each year since treatment, how large those effects were and when they peaked, and how the per-polygon peak years distribute across treatments and ecoregions. Read the two halves as separate questions - a year can carry a high significance rate with small effects, or the reverse.

How does time since treatment affect significance?

This section attempts to answer two questions:

  1. How often does a significant effect show up in a given year? The stacked-direction figure immediately below.

  2. How large are those effects? The mean-effect table and figure further down. A year can have a handful of significant pixels that each moved a long way, or many pixels that each moved a little, and those are different results.

No weighting is used anywhere in this section. The mean effect per year is a plain arithmetic mean of effect over the significant pixels in that year, split by direction of effect, so the reported peak is the year whose significant pixels actually moved furthest rather than a significance-weighted compromise across the whole time series. Some weighting methods were checked and did not improve the results - see weight_testing_summary.Rmd for that analysis.

Everything in this section is drawn on the truncated series: for this objective no year fell below the 10-significant-pixel threshold, so the full record to year 33 is used. This is what stops a peak year being reported from the part of the record where almost nothing was significant; it also means the x axis here can end earlier than another objective’s, so the two are not read off the same range.

Figure. X axis: years since treatment, one bar per year, labelled every 5 years. Y axis: the percentage of that year’s pixels with a significant DART effect - the full height of a bar is the year’s overall % significant, and it is a percentage of all pixels observed in that year, not of the significant ones. Fill: the direction of the significant effect, splitting each bar into a blue significant negative component and a red significant positive component; the intended direction for this objective (positive) is the segment drawn against the axis, with the unintended direction stacked above it. Fill colours mean the same thing in every direction figure in this report. There are no facets or other groupings.

Two different sample sizes are labelled on each bar, and they are not meant to sum to each other:

  • The rotated label sitting above each bar is that year’s group total - every pixel observed in that year, significant or not. It says how much data is behind the bar, and it is the denominator of the percentage on the Y axis.
  • The white label inside each stacked segment is the number of pixels that were significant and in that segment’s direction. These two are the sample sizes behind the two segment heights themselves.

So the two segment labels add up to the number of significant pixels in that year, which is generally far smaller than the group total above the bar, because most pixels in a year are not significant. Reading down a tall bar with a small group total is therefore a different situation from a short bar with a large one, which is exactly why both numbers are drawn. Segments too short to hold their label legibly are left unlabelled to avoid white text spilling onto the panel background.

  • Treatment was most effective (highest % significant pixels) at year 33 (41.4% significant).
  • Treatment was least effective (lowest % significant pixels) at year 29 (11.8% significant).

The shaded band around each line is that year × direction mean ± 1 SE: it is sampling uncertainty in the mean effect, not the spread of individual pixel effects, so it narrows mainly where a year has many significant pixels. Dashed vertical lines mark each direction’s peak year from the table above, labelled with the mean effect at the peak, its SE, and the number of significant pixels behind it.   • Significant positive effects were largest at year 33 (mean effect 23.4308, SE 2.3622, n = 17 significant pixels), which is the last year observed for that direction - the effect may still have been growing past the end of the record.

Note that the year with the largest mean effect need not be the year with the most significant pixels: the two questions can peak at different times, and a peak that lands on the last observed year is flagged as censored above for the same reason as in the by-polygon table further down.

Each polygon is reduced to the single year in which its own % significant pixels was highest (“peak significance year”); those per-polygon peak years are then summarized across polygons, by treatment in the first table and by ecoregion in the second. Note that “last year observed” now means the last year retained after the late-year truncation described above, so where a series was truncated the censoring flag is partly an artefact of the threshold rather than of the record itself - it marks the end of the analysable series, not necessarily the end of the data. What that censoring implies is taken up under Interpretation at the end of the report.

Table. One row for this objective x cover response. % Pixels Lost is the combined cost of all three filters, not the cell filter alone. # Tx Absent / # Eco Absent count levels missing from the post-filter data for any reason, which is a different quantity from the two depopulated columns: a level that only ever appeared in sparse cells disappears without the depopulation filter being involved.

Post-filter, this objective x cover response retains 605946 pixels across 12 treatment level(s) and 22 ecoregion level(s), the smallest surviving totals being 1035 pixels for a treatment and 484 for an ecoregion, against a per-cell threshold of 300.

Interpretation
  • Significance patterns over fine objectives are highly heterogenous, but too complex to interpret casually.
  • Significance patterns over treatments are also highly heterogenous, but similarily complex.
  • Significance patterns over ecoregion probably require some environmental context, or an expert eye.
  • Time effects look to be very positive earlier in the treatment (< 20 YST) but then become negative after that, indicating a potential regression of treatment effects
  • Treatment looked generally successful
  • CLAUDE: The largest base in the report (605,946 pixels, 539 polygons) and the second-strongest margin: 20.7% intended against 3.8% unintended, 5.4:1.
  • CLAUDE: The regression noted above is visible in the year bins, but as two separate movements rather than a sign flip: the intended rate falls from 27.84% in years 1-5 to 10.94% at 16+ while the unintended rate rises from 3.52% to 6.01%, so the ratio collapses from 7.9:1 to 1.8:1. The magnitude side agrees - the unintended peak mean sits at year 21 (-10.6, n = 733 significant pixels). Stating it as decay plus a real accumulation of opposite-sign pixels is better supported than stating it as an average that turns negative.
  • CLAUDE: The intended peak of 23.4 at year 33 is flagged censored and rests on 17 significant pixels - the only censored peak in the document. It cannot be read as a late resurgence; it marks the end of the analysable series for that direction.
  • CLAUDE: The treatment ordering repeats decrease_tre’s, which is the cross-objective pattern worth reporting: seeding;vegetation removal leads at 39.94% intended, the largest treatment by area (seeding;soil disturbance, 165,121 pixels) returns 28.53%, and prescribed burn sits at 9.70% on 155,032 pixels (rank 10 of 12). Adding mechanical disturbance to seeding roughly doubles the intended rate; burning with or before seeding does not.
  • CLAUDE: On the ecoregion axis, the environmental context asked for above should start from the fact that the top cell is small: High Elevation Carbonate Mountains at 87.13% intended holds 1,974 pixels, 0.3% of the objective. The ordering is informative at the large end (Semiarid Benchlands and Canyonlands, 229,443 pixels, 17.59%) and noisy at both extremes.

Results after all three filters

The pixel cutoff for each (treatment × ecoregion) combination was 300.

Three filters have now been applied to this objective x cover response, in this order, and the percentage below is the combined cost of all three:

  1. Sparse (treatment x ecoregion) cells - the 27 combinations listed above, below 300 pixels each.
  2. Depopulated treatment or ecoregion levels - on, at the same 300-pixel threshold: 0 treatment and 0 ecoregion level(s) removed. This catches a level thinned across many surviving cells, which the cell filter cannot see.
  3. Late-year truncation - no year fell below 10 significant pixels, so the series was not truncated.

Total data lost across all three: 1.20%. Treatment levels absent from the post-filter data: prescribed burn;seeding. Ecoregion levels absent: Eastern Mojave Low Ranges and Arid Footslopes, High Elevation Forests and Shrublands, Malad and Cache Valleys, Sub-Irrigated High Valleys, Mid-Elevation Uinta Mountains, Wetlands, Uinta Basin Floor, Arid Canyonlands. (These are levels gone for any reason - a level that only ever appeared in sparse cells disappears without the depopulation filter being involved.)

Significant DART effects, through time

The same effects along the time axis and against the covariates that interact with it: how often a significant effect occurred in each year since treatment, how large those effects were and when they peaked, and how the per-polygon peak years distribute across treatments and ecoregions. Read the two halves as separate questions - a year can carry a high significance rate with small effects, or the reverse.

How does time since treatment affect significance?

This section attempts to answer two questions:

  1. How often does a significant effect show up in a given year? The stacked-direction figure immediately below.

  2. How large are those effects? The mean-effect table and figure further down. A year can have a handful of significant pixels that each moved a long way, or many pixels that each moved a little, and those are different results.

No weighting is used anywhere in this section. The mean effect per year is a plain arithmetic mean of effect over the significant pixels in that year, split by direction of effect, so the reported peak is the year whose significant pixels actually moved furthest rather than a significance-weighted compromise across the whole time series. Some weighting methods were checked and did not improve the results - see weight_testing_summary.Rmd for that analysis.

Everything in this section is drawn on the truncated series: for this objective no year fell below the 10-significant-pixel threshold, so the full record to year 30 is used. This is what stops a peak year being reported from the part of the record where almost nothing was significant; it also means the x axis here can end earlier than another objective’s, so the two are not read off the same range.

Figure. X axis: years since treatment, one bar per year, labelled every 5 years. Y axis: the percentage of that year’s pixels with a significant DART effect - the full height of a bar is the year’s overall % significant, and it is a percentage of all pixels observed in that year, not of the significant ones. Fill: the direction of the significant effect, splitting each bar into a blue significant negative component and a red significant positive component; the intended direction for this objective (positive) is the segment drawn against the axis, with the unintended direction stacked above it. Fill colours mean the same thing in every direction figure in this report. There are no facets or other groupings.

Two different sample sizes are labelled on each bar, and they are not meant to sum to each other:

  • The rotated label sitting above each bar is that year’s group total - every pixel observed in that year, significant or not. It says how much data is behind the bar, and it is the denominator of the percentage on the Y axis.
  • The white label inside each stacked segment is the number of pixels that were significant and in that segment’s direction. These two are the sample sizes behind the two segment heights themselves.

So the two segment labels add up to the number of significant pixels in that year, which is generally far smaller than the group total above the bar, because most pixels in a year are not significant. Reading down a tall bar with a small group total is therefore a different situation from a short bar with a large one, which is exactly why both numbers are drawn. Segments too short to hold their label legibly are left unlabelled to avoid white text spilling onto the panel background.

  • Treatment was most effective (highest % significant pixels) at year 2 (31.1% significant).
  • Treatment was least effective (lowest % significant pixels) at year 22 (15.1% significant).

Figure. X axis: years since treatment. Y axis: the mean DART effect (Δ RAP cover) among significant pixels only in that year, computed separately for each direction - so the two series sit either side of the zero line by construction and are never averaged into a single number. Colour: direction of the effect (red = significant positive, blue = significant negative), using the same colours as the stacked figure above. The shaded band around each line is that year × direction mean ± 1 SE: it is sampling uncertainty in the mean effect, not the spread of individual pixel effects, so it narrows mainly where a year has many significant pixels. A year × direction cell backed by a single significant pixel has no SE and is drawn as a bare point, keeping the line through it unbroken. Dashed vertical lines mark each direction’s peak year from the table above, labelled with the mean effect at the peak, its SE, and the number of significant pixels behind it. Non-significant pixels are excluded outright rather than entered as zeros, and no weighting is applied anywhere. There are no facets or other groupings.

  • Significant negative effects were largest at year 2 (mean effect -11.8737, SE 0.1131, n = 2907 significant pixels).
  • Significant positive effects were largest at year 20 (mean effect 14.0138, SE 0.3377, n = 378 significant pixels).

Note that the year with the largest mean effect need not be the year with the most significant pixels: the two questions can peak at different times, and a peak that lands on the last observed year is flagged as censored above for the same reason as in the by-polygon table further down.

Each polygon is reduced to the single year in which its own % significant pixels was highest (“peak significance year”); those per-polygon peak years are then summarized across polygons, by treatment in the first table and by ecoregion in the second. Columns: number of polygons behind the row, mean / SD / min / max of the peak year, and the percentage of polygons whose peak fell on the last year they were observed. A polygon’s peak year is flagged as “censored” in those cases, because we can’t rule out that significance was still rising beyond the end of the available time series. Note that “last year observed” now means the last year retained after the late-year truncation described above, so where a series was truncated the censoring flag is partly an artefact of the threshold rather than of the record itself - it marks the end of the analysable series, not necessarily the end of the data. What that censoring implies is taken up under Interpretation at the end of the report.

Overall results and interpretation

Summary statistics

What the three sample-size filters cost this objective x cover response, in one row - the same quantities reported in prose under Results after all three filters above, gathered here so that this subsection stands on its own. The identical row appears in the cross-objective filtering log in 2_make_DART_results.Rmd, where it can be read against the other objectives.

Objective Cover Min Pixels per Tx x Eco # Tx x Eco Excluded # Tx Depopulated # Eco Depopulated Min Pixels per Year Year Truncated At # Years Dropped % Pixels Lost # Tx Absent # Eco Absent
increase_shr SHR 300 27 0 0 10 NA 0 1.2 1 8

Table. One row for this objective x cover response. % Pixels Lost is the combined cost of all three filters, not the cell filter alone. # Tx Absent / # Eco Absent count levels missing from the post-filter data for any reason, which is a different quantity from the two depopulated columns: a level that only ever appeared in sparse cells disappears without the depopulation filter being involved.

Post-filter, this objective x cover response retains 285880 pixels across 12 treatment level(s) and 19 ecoregion level(s), the smallest surviving totals being 1059 pixels for a treatment and 313 for an ecoregion, against a per-cell threshold of 300.

Interpretation
  • Mostly same considerations as increase_pfg
  • Time effects are negative immediately after treatment, then stay generally positive
  • Treatment looked generally successful.
  • CLAUDE: Call this the weakest of the four objectives that came out in the intended direction rather than a straightforward success: 14.9% intended against 8.6% unintended is only 1.7:1, so roughly a third of the significant pixels moved the wrong way.
  • CLAUDE: The knock-down-then-recover reading above is the best-supported timing statement in the report, because both sides of it rest on large samples: the unintended peak is at year 2 (-11.9, n = 2907 significant pixels, the largest count behind any peak in the document) against an intended peak at year 20 (14.0, n = 378). The year bins agree - the unintended rate falls from 11.20% to 6.73% across the record while the intended rate falls more slowly, 17.98% to 11.01%.
  • CLAUDE: This objective is not an independent sample in any meaningful sense - 0.88% of its pixels carry no other objective and 89.03% also carry increase_pfg. It is best reported as the shrub-response arm of the same treatments increase_pfg describes. It also shares 16.53% of its pixels with decrease_afg, whose unintended positive result is the opposite reading of overlapping ground.
  • CLAUDE: The treatment ordering does not repeat the pattern seen for increase_pfg and decrease_tre, and that is worth stating as a difference rather than smoothing over. The top rate (soil disturbance, 32.24%) sits on only 2,100 pixels, and the two largest treatments diverge the wrong way: seeding at 82,001 pixels returns 15.35% while seeding;soil disturbance at 77,788 pixels returns 12.37%. Adding soil disturbance to seeding does not help shrub recovery the way it helps perennial grass. prescribed burn is again near the bottom (7.38%, rank 11 of 12).
  • CLAUDE: The top ecoregion here (High Elevation Carbonate Mountains, 76.80% intended on 1,974 pixels) is the same cell that tops increase_pfg, so one small high-elevation area drives the best result for both shrub and perennial-grass increase. Confirming it is a real effect rather than a sampling artefact needs either the environmental context or more pixels from that ecoregion.

Overall results and interpretation, all objectives

The five objective x cover response sections above each end with their own summary statistics and interpretation, written next to the evidence they describe. This section puts the same material side by side, which is where one objective can be read against another. Nothing here is a second copy: the filtering table is compiled from the same per-objective rows, and the interpretation text is emitted from the same character vectors those sections define, so the two presentations cannot disagree.

Two standing caveats apply to everything below. The objective groupings are not a partition - a pixel counts toward an objective if it fell in any part of that objective, so multi-objective treatments appear in several groupings and parts of the dataset are counted more than once. And an objective/response pairing is only included when the response cover type matches the objective’s target cover, with bare ground the sole exception.

Interpretation by objective

cover: AFG , objective: decrease afg

  • This was the only objective that achieved mostly the opposite of what it intended in that the direction of effect was usually positive, while the attempted effect was negative. I would hypothesize that the very strong unintended-effect result has to do with disturbance effects or the interact effects of compound objectives.
  • Significance patterns over fine objectives are highly heterogenous, but too complex to interpret casually.
  • Significance patterns over treatments are also highly heterogenous, but similarily complex.
  • Significance patterns over ecoregion probably require some environmental context, or an expert eye. For example I don’t have enough personal knowledge to guess why Uinta Basin Floor was so much higher than the other ecoregions.”
  • Treatment was generally not successful.
  • CLAUDE: The unintended direction dominates by a factor of 4.2 (22.7% of pixels unintended against 5.4% intended), and it dominates in every year bin: the ratio narrows from 5.1:1 in years 1-5 to 2.2:1 at 16+ but never reverses. So the result is not an early transient that later resolves - it is the standing pattern for this objective across the whole record.
  • CLAUDE: The compound-objective explanation offered above is consistent with the overlap structure: only 5.68% of these pixels carry no other objective, while 79.17% also carry increase_pfg. This section is therefore not an independent sample - it is largely the same ground the other objectives report, read against a different goal.
  • CLAUDE: The ecoregion spread is driven by small cells and should be read as a hypothesis-generating list, not a ranking. The top ecoregion (Uinta Basin Floor, 25.79% intended) holds 1,008 pixels, 1.2% of this objective’s 84,175, while the pixel-weighted rate for the objective as a whole is 5.4%. Any statement about the objective should quote the weighted rate.
  • CLAUDE: Within the treatment axis the ordering is interpretable even if the levels are heterogeneous: vegetation removal ranks first at 14.06% intended, with 1 of 6 treatments above 10%, and the largest treatment by area - seeding, 27,645 pixels - returns 1.87%. Where intended reductions in annual grass did occur they involved physically removing or disturbing vegetation rather than seeding alone.
  • CLAUDE: Do not read timing off the peak-magnitude table for this objective. The intended peak (-43.3 at year 18) rests on 132 significant pixels and the unintended peak (28.8 at year 25) on 10, both late in a record truncated at year 27. The per-polygon peak-significance years are early by contrast (treatment means of 2.8-6.2 years), so the frequency of a significant effect peaks early and decays while the large late means come from very few pixels.

cover: SHR , objective: decrease shr

  • Treatment looked successful, but at a smaller magnitude than the other objectives
  • needs more details
  • CLAUDE: The frequency evidence supports the reading above: the intended direction outnumbers the unintended one 2.2:1 (10.3% against 4.7%), the second-narrowest margin among the four objectives whose result went in the intended direction, and the intended peak mean effect is -21.4 in Δ RAP cover units at year 1 (n = 2455 significant pixels).
  • CLAUDE: The objective-level rate is effectively one treatment’s rate on one ecoregion. prescribed burn carries 124,020 of the 186,596 pixels (66%) at 8.65% intended, and Semiarid Benchlands and Canyonlands carries 132,266 (71%) at 8.79%; the higher rates in those tables - seeding at 24.15% and Sagebrush Basins and Slopes at 29.45% - each sit on a few percent of the pixels. The 10.3% headline should be attributed accordingly rather than read as a general result for shrub reduction.
  • CLAUDE: The response is immediate and then erodes rather than building: the intended peak falls at year 1, the earliest of any objective, and the intended rate declines monotonically from 17.32% in years 1-5 to 6.54% at 16+. Nothing here suggests a lagged shrub reduction.
  • CLAUDE: Ignore the unintended peak of 14.2 at year 27 - it is backed by n = 1 significant pixels and has no SE, so it is a single-pixel artefact of averaging over significant pixels only, not a late reversal. The late-year truncation at year 33 does not catch it, because that filter counts across both directions.
  • CLAUDE: This objective has the thinnest polygon base of the five - 61 polygons across 11 treatments, with up to 50% of a treatment’s polygons censored at their last observed year - so the per-polygon peak-year summaries are indicative only. 95.41% of its pixels carry another objective (85.21% also increase_pfg), which means the shrub reduction cannot be separated from the treatments those objectives describe.

cover: TRE , objective: decrease tre

  • To be written.
  • CLAUDE: This is the strongest and cleanest result in the report. The intended direction outnumbers the unintended one 5.6:1 (25.6% against 4.6%) on the largest pixel base of the five (556,499), and it is the only objective where a substantial share of pixels - 38.12% - carries no other objective, so it is the one result that is close to an independent sample.
  • CLAUDE: Read its covariate tables with the threshold in mind. This objective’s per-cell floor is 10 pixels against 300 for the other four, and no cell, level or year was dropped (0.00% of pixels lost), so its treatment and ecoregion tables retain cells the other sections would have removed - the smallest surviving ecoregion row is 16 pixels. The extreme rates at the top of the ecoregion table are those cells; the pixel-weighted rate is 25.6%.
  • CLAUDE: The treatment ordering is the clearest management signal in the document. Every combination of seeding with mechanical work sits at the top - seeding;vegetation removal leads at 51.44% intended - while prescribed burn alone returns 11.59% on 154,865 pixels (rank 11 of 13) and the largest treatment by area, vegetation removal (218,327 pixels), returns 22.89%. Mechanical removal paired with seeding is 2.2 times the intended rate of removal alone and 4.4 times the rate of burning.
  • CLAUDE: The decay through time is the one finding that generalises across all five objectives, though what the unintended rate does alongside it differs: here the intended rate falls from 34.73% in years 1-5 to 11.89% at 16+ while the unintended rate rises from 2.82% to 6.88%, so the intended-to-unintended ratio collapses from 12:1 to 1.7:1. Detectable tree-cover reduction is a property of the first decade after treatment.
  • CLAUDE: The peak means are late (-26.6 at year 29 intended, 14.2 at year 31 unintended) but rest on 100 and 27 significant pixels against 556,499 in total, and no year was truncated here, so the tail of the record is retained at very small per-year samples. Treat the peak years as poorly determined and lean on the year-bin table for timing instead.

cover: PFG , objective: increase pfg

  • Significance patterns over fine objectives are highly heterogenous, but too complex to interpret casually.
  • Significance patterns over treatments are also highly heterogenous, but similarily complex.
  • Significance patterns over ecoregion probably require some environmental context, or an expert eye.
  • Time effects look to be very positive earlier in the treatment (< 20 YST) but then become negative after that, indicating a potential regression of treatment effects
  • Treatment looked generally successful
  • CLAUDE: The largest base in the report (605,946 pixels, 539 polygons) and the second-strongest margin: 20.7% intended against 3.8% unintended, 5.4:1.
  • CLAUDE: The regression noted above is visible in the year bins, but as two separate movements rather than a sign flip: the intended rate falls from 27.84% in years 1-5 to 10.94% at 16+ while the unintended rate rises from 3.52% to 6.01%, so the ratio collapses from 7.9:1 to 1.8:1. The magnitude side agrees - the unintended peak mean sits at year 21 (-10.6, n = 733 significant pixels). Stating it as decay plus a real accumulation of opposite-sign pixels is better supported than stating it as an average that turns negative.
  • CLAUDE: The intended peak of 23.4 at year 33 is flagged censored and rests on 17 significant pixels - the only censored peak in the document. It cannot be read as a late resurgence; it marks the end of the analysable series for that direction.
  • CLAUDE: The treatment ordering repeats decrease_tre’s, which is the cross-objective pattern worth reporting: seeding;vegetation removal leads at 39.94% intended, the largest treatment by area (seeding;soil disturbance, 165,121 pixels) returns 28.53%, and prescribed burn sits at 9.70% on 155,032 pixels (rank 10 of 12). Adding mechanical disturbance to seeding roughly doubles the intended rate; burning with or before seeding does not.
  • CLAUDE: On the ecoregion axis, the environmental context asked for above should start from the fact that the top cell is small: High Elevation Carbonate Mountains at 87.13% intended holds 1,974 pixels, 0.3% of the objective. The ordering is informative at the large end (Semiarid Benchlands and Canyonlands, 229,443 pixels, 17.59%) and noisy at both extremes.

cover: SHR , objective: increase shr

  • Mostly same considerations as increase_pfg
  • Time effects are negative immediately after treatment, then stay generally positive
  • Treatment looked generally successful.
  • CLAUDE: Call this the weakest of the four objectives that came out in the intended direction rather than a straightforward success: 14.9% intended against 8.6% unintended is only 1.7:1, so roughly a third of the significant pixels moved the wrong way.
  • CLAUDE: The knock-down-then-recover reading above is the best-supported timing statement in the report, because both sides of it rest on large samples: the unintended peak is at year 2 (-11.9, n = 2907 significant pixels, the largest count behind any peak in the document) against an intended peak at year 20 (14.0, n = 378). The year bins agree - the unintended rate falls from 11.20% to 6.73% across the record while the intended rate falls more slowly, 17.98% to 11.01%.
  • CLAUDE: This objective is not an independent sample in any meaningful sense - 0.88% of its pixels carry no other objective and 89.03% also carry increase_pfg. It is best reported as the shrub-response arm of the same treatments increase_pfg describes. It also shares 16.53% of its pixels with decrease_afg, whose unintended positive result is the opposite reading of overlapping ground.
  • CLAUDE: The treatment ordering does not repeat the pattern seen for increase_pfg and decrease_tre, and that is worth stating as a difference rather than smoothing over. The top rate (soil disturbance, 32.24%) sits on only 2,100 pixels, and the two largest treatments diverge the wrong way: seeding at 82,001 pixels returns 15.35% while seeding;soil disturbance at 77,788 pixels returns 12.37%. Adding soil disturbance to seeding does not help shrub recovery the way it helps perennial grass. prescribed burn is again near the bottom (7.38%, rank 11 of 12).
  • CLAUDE: The top ecoregion here (High Elevation Carbonate Mountains, 76.80% intended on 1,974 pixels) is the same cell that tops increase_pfg, so one small high-elevation area drives the best result for both shrub and perennial-grass increase. Confirming it is a real effect rather than a sampling artefact needs either the environmental context or more pixels from that ecoregion.
